data.headline: Your Brain is Lying to You About Procrastination
data.subheadline: It's not laziness—it's a protection mechanism gone wrong

data.title: Why We Procrastinate
data.body: When you procrastinate, your brain is trying to protect you from perceived threats. But modern threats (deadlines, responsibilities) trigger the same fight-or-flight response as ancient dangers. Your amygdala hijacks rational thinking, making 'later' feel safer than 'now'.
data.highlight: Procrastination is emotional regulation, not time management

data.myth: Procrastinators are just lazy and need more discipline
data.fact: Procrastination is linked to anxiety, perfectionism, and fear of failure—not character flaws
data.proof: Research shows procrastinators have higher activity in the amygdala (emotion center) when facing tasks

data.context: of college students report procrastinating on academic work regularly
data.takeaway: Nearly everyone struggles with it—you're not broken

data.callToAction: Ready to understand your mind better?
data.subtext: Follow for psychology insights that actually make sense

caption:
Your brain isn't lazy—it's scared. Here's the neuroscience behind procrastination and why 'just do it' advice fails.

Procrastination activates your amygdala (fear center), not your prefrontal cortex (planning center). That's why willpower alone doesn't work.

The fix? Reduce the emotional threat. Break tasks into tiny steps, forgive past delays, and focus on starting—not finishing.
